21	This playbook reflects Clearwater Securities\' firm standard positions for review of issuer-prepared indentures in Rule 144A / Regulation S high-yield secured notes offerings. All reviewing associates must apply these positions as baseline requirements when marking up issuer drafts. Deviations from these positions require partner approval. This document is intended solely for use by the Aldgate & Whitmore deal team and the Clearwater Securities leveraged finance group, and its contents must not be disclosed to issuers, issuers\' counsel, co-managers not listed above, or any other third party without the prior written consent of both David K. Morrow and Samantha Voss.
22	
23	**[I. GENERAL INSTRUCTIONS AND REVIEW METHODOLOGY]{.underline}**
24	
25	**Purpose.** This document sets forth the mandatory positions that Clearwater Securities LLC (\"Clearwater\") requires its outside counsel, Aldgate & Whitmore LLP, to advance in every high-yield indenture negotiation on which Clearwater serves as an initial purchaser, lead-left bookrunner, or joint bookrunner. These positions represent Clearwater\'s assessment of institutional investor expectations and market-standard protections for holders of high-yield notes issued in the 144A / Regulation S market. They have been developed through Clearwater\'s extensive experience as a leading underwriter of healthcare leveraged finance transactions and are informed by feedback from Clearwater\'s institutional investor base, including dedicated high-yield funds, crossover accounts, and CLO managers. The positions set forth herein are intended to serve as a floor, not a ceiling, for noteholder protections.
26	
27	**Directive to Reviewing Associates.** All reviewing associates assigned to an indenture markup must compare each provision of the issuer draft against the corresponding section of this playbook. Any deviation from the playbook position must be redlined in the issuer draft with a margin comment that includes the following four elements:
28	
29	> \(a\) a clear statement of the **issue** --- what the issuer draft says and why it deviates from the playbook;
30	>
31	> \(b\) the applicable **playbook position** --- what Clearwater requires the provision to say;
32	>
33	> \(c\) a brief **rationale** --- the credit, structural, or legal reason for the Clearwater position; and
34	>
35	> \(d\) a **severity classification** assigned from the three-tier system described below.
36	
37	**Severity Classification System.** Each issue identified in the markup must be classified according to the following system:
38	
39	> • **Critical** --- Must-have provision. This position represents a deal-breaker if not obtained. If the issuer or issuer\'s counsel refuses to accept the Clearwater position on a Critical item, the reviewing associate must immediately escalate the issue to the supervising partner. No Critical item may be conceded without the express approval of both the Aldgate & Whitmore supervising partner and the Clearwater deal team.
40	>
41	> • **Significant** --- Strongly preferred provision. This position represents the current Clearwater standard and reflects best market practice. If the issuer resists, the associate must escalate to the supervising partner for discussion. Significant items may be traded against other Significant items in the context of overall package negotiations, but only with partner approval.
42	>
43	> • **Moderate** --- Preferred but negotiable provision. This position reflects best practice but deviation may be tolerable in the context of overall deal dynamics and other concessions obtained. The associate must document the rationale for any Moderate item not pursued.
44	
45	**Focus of Review.** Do not mark up provisions that conform to this playbook or that represent standard market terms not addressed herein. Focus review time on the following articles and sections, which present the most frequent areas of deviation between issuer drafts and Clearwater\'s requirements: definitions (Article 1, with particular focus on Consolidated EBITDA, Permitted Indebtedness, and Restricted Payments definitions), covenants (Article 4, including incurrence of indebtedness, restricted payments, asset sales, affiliate transactions, and reporting), Events of Default (Article 6), and Collateral provisions (Article 10 and the related Security Documents and Intercreditor Agreement).
46	
47	**Healthcare-Specific Caution.** Issuer\'s counsel in healthcare leveraged finance transactions frequently push aggressive baskets and extended time periods, often justified by reference to the capital-intensive and acquisition-driven nature of the healthcare industry. Associates should scrutinize all dollar thresholds, percentages, ratio tests, and cure/grace periods with particular care. Adjustments characterized as \"industry standard for healthcare issuers\" are not automatically acceptable; each must be measured against the specific positions in this playbook.
48	
49	**Cross-Reference.** Associates should cross-reference all indenture provisions against the offering term sheet and preliminary offering memorandum to confirm consistency of financial terms, pricing assumptions, and structural features. Any discrepancy between the indenture and the term sheet or OC must be flagged and resolved before the indenture is finalized.
50	
51	**[II. DEFINITION OF \"CONSOLIDATED EBITDA\" / \"ADJUSTED EBITDA\"]{.underline}**
52	
53	**Severity: CRITICAL**
54	
55	**Position.** The definition of Consolidated EBITDA (or Adjusted EBITDA, however labeled in the issuer draft) must include a cap on pro forma cost savings, operating improvements, and synergies addbacks. The cap must not exceed **25% of Consolidated EBITDA**, calculated before giving effect to such addbacks. This cap applies to the aggregate of all pro forma adjustments for cost savings, operating improvements, synergies, and similar addbacks, whether arising from acquisitions, dispositions, facility closures, restructurings, operational initiatives, or any other event or circumstance. If the issuer draft applies different labels to different categories of addbacks (e.g., \"run-rate cost savings,\" \"operational synergies,\" \"restructuring adjustments,\" \"pro forma operating improvements\"), all such categories must be brought within the single aggregate 25% cap. The purpose of the cap is to prevent artificial inflation of EBITDA, which would loosen every ratio-based test in the indenture.
56	
57	**Run-Rate Period.** Any projected cost savings or synergies must be required to be realized or reasonably expected to be realized within **18 months** of the date of the transaction or event giving rise to such adjustment. The 18-month realization window is the maximum acceptable period for purposes of this playbook. Any run-rate period exceeding 18 months --- including the 24-month periods that have become increasingly common in recent healthcare leveraged finance indentures --- must be redlined down to 18 months. The run-rate period must be clearly stated in the definition and must apply uniformly to all categories of pro forma addbacks.
58	
59	**Certification Requirement.** All pro forma addbacks for projected cost savings, operating improvements, and synergies must be **factually supportable** and **certified by the Chief Financial Officer** of the Issuer in a certificate delivered to the Trustee. The certification must affirm that such adjustments are (i) based on good-faith estimates prepared by the Issuer\'s management, (ii) supported by underlying documentation available for review by the Trustee upon request, and (iii) reasonably expected to be realized within the applicable run-rate period. The CFO certification requirement serves both a governance function (imposing personal accountability on a senior officer) and an evidentiary function (creating a documented record of the factual basis for each addback). If the issuer draft omits this certification requirement, it must be added.
60	
61	**Rationale:**
62	
63	> • Uncapped synergy addbacks allow issuers to inflate EBITDA artificially, loosening every ratio-based test in the indenture, including the debt incurrence ratio test, the restricted payments builder basket, and the Consolidated Total Leverage Ratio.
64	>
65	> • The 25% cap is consistent with recent market precedent in BB/Ba rated secured healthcare issuances, including the Memorial Regional Health System notes (2024), the Lakewood Medical Centers senior secured notes (2024), and the Broadview Healthcare Holdings exchange offer (2023).
66	>
67	> • An 18-month realization window is the maximum acceptable period; longer windows create material credit risk by crediting savings that may never materialize and that, in Clearwater\'s experience, frequently do not materialize within the extended time frame.
68	>
69	> • CFO certification provides a governance check and potential liability anchor for misleading projections, giving noteholders and the Trustee a basis for challenging addbacks that prove to have been without factual foundation.
70	
71	**Common Issuer Tactics.** Watch for the following:
72	
73	> \(a\) No cap at all on pro forma addbacks --- the definition permits unlimited addbacks, which can result in a stated EBITDA figure that bears no relationship to actual cash earnings;
74	>
75	> \(b\) Run-rate periods of 24 months or longer, sometimes tied to the anniversary of the relevant transaction rather than the date of the financial reporting period;
76	>
77	> \(c\) Missing CFO certification requirement, or a certification that is qualified by phrases such as \"to the knowledge of\" or \"in the reasonable judgment of,\" which dilute accountability;
78	>
79	> \(d\) Addbacks for \"anticipated\" or \"expected\" improvements without any requirement that such improvements be factually supportable, reasonably quantifiable, or tied to a specific identified action or initiative.
80	
81	This definition underlies every financial ratio in the indenture. An overbroad definition can render all ratio-based covenants meaningless. Accordingly, this is classified as a Critical position and any deviation must be escalated immediately.
82	
83	**[III. LIMITATION ON INCURRENCE OF INDEBTEDNESS]{.underline}**
84	
85	**III.A --- Ratio Debt Incurrence Test**
86	
87	**Severity: CRITICAL**
88	
89	**Position.** The covenant must permit incurrence of ratio debt only if, after giving pro forma effect to such incurrence and the application of proceeds therefrom, the Issuer\'s Fixed Charge Coverage Ratio is at least **2.00 to 1.00**, calculated on a pro forma basis as if such Indebtedness had been incurred and the proceeds therefrom had been applied at the beginning of the most recent four consecutive fiscal quarter period for which internal financial statements are available at the time of such incurrence. The ratio must be tested at the time of incurrence and the Issuer must deliver to the Trustee an Officer\'s Certificate demonstrating compliance with the ratio test.
90	
91	**Pro Forma Requirement.** The indenture must explicitly state that the ratio test gives pro forma effect to the Indebtedness being incurred and the application of proceeds therefrom. This is a fundamental mechanical requirement. If the issuer draft permits ratio debt incurrence without including the new debt in the Fixed Charge Coverage Ratio calculation --- that is, if the test is applied on a \"before giving effect\" basis or is simply silent on the pro forma methodology --- this must be flagged as a Critical deficiency and corrected. The omission of a pro forma requirement for the debt being incurred is one of the most dangerous drafting deficiencies in an indenture, because it permits the issuer to layer on unlimited debt in sequential transactions, each tested against the pre-existing capital structure, with no single test ever capturing the aggregate incremental leverage.
92	
93	**Rationale:**
94	
95	> • Without a pro forma test that includes the debt being incurred, the ratio test fails to serve its fundamental purpose of constraining aggregate leverage. An issuer with a 2.50x Fixed Charge Coverage Ratio could theoretically incur unlimited new debt in a series of transactions, each individually tested against the same pre-incurrence ratio, without the cumulative effect of such incurrences ever being captured by the test.
96	>
97	> • This is a fundamental investor protection. Its omission represents a significant drafting deficiency that must be corrected regardless of whether issuer\'s counsel characterizes it as intentional or inadvertent.
98	>
99	> • In Clearwater\'s experience, the omission is sometimes the result of careless drafting but is occasionally intentional, particularly where the issuer anticipates a near-term acquisition program. Either way, it is unacceptable.
100	
101	**III.B --- Credit Facility Basket**
102	
103	**Severity: CRITICAL**
104	
105	**Position.** The permitted indebtedness basket for Credit Facility debt (including revolving credit facilities, term loans, and letter of credit facilities) must be capped at the **greater of \$850 million and 1.10x LTM Adjusted EBITDA** (where LTM Adjusted EBITDA is calculated for the most recently ended four fiscal quarter period for which financial statements are available). This basket includes all Indebtedness incurred under the Credit Facility, whether in the form of revolving loans, term loans, letters of credit, or other extensions of credit, and is measured on a committed (not drawn) basis.
106	
107	**Rationale:**
108	
109	> • The credit facility basket directly impacts the quantum of debt that can be incurred senior to or pari passu with the Notes outside of ratio discipline. Because debt incurred under the credit facility basket is not subject to the Fixed Charge Coverage Ratio test, the size of this basket is a critical determinant of the issuer\'s ability to lever up without covenant restraint.
110	>
111	> • A dollar cap of \$850 million is appropriate for an issuer of this credit profile (BB-/Ba3 rated, mid-cap hospital operator with approximately \$770 million in LTM EBITDA).
112	>
113	> • The 1.10x ratio component provides a growing basket tied to earnings growth without creating excessive headroom. As the issuer\'s EBITDA grows, the credit facility basket grows proportionally, maintaining a disciplined relationship between the two.
114	>
115	> • Watch for inflated dollar caps (e.g., \$1 billion or more) or inflated ratios (e.g., 1.25x, 1.50x, or higher) that allow the credit facility to grow disproportionately relative to the issuer\'s earnings. Issuers and their counsel frequently justify larger baskets by reference to the capital-intensive nature of hospital operations; this justification is not sufficient to override the playbook standard.
116	
117	**III.C --- General Debt Basket**
118	
119	**Severity: SIGNIFICANT**
120	
121	**Position.** Any general or catch-all indebtedness basket must not exceed the **greater of \$100 million and 13% of Total Assets** (calculated as of the most recent balance sheet date for which financial statements are available). This basket permits incurrence of Indebtedness that does not fit within any other specified basket and is not subject to the ratio test or any other financial condition.
122	
123	**Rationale.** The general debt basket is uncapped by ratio tests and functions as a free-and-clear basket. Its purpose is to provide operational flexibility for routine indebtedness needs that do not justify the complexity of ratio test compliance. However, an excessive general basket undermines the entire debt incurrence framework by permitting meaningful leverage increases without any financial test. The proposed thresholds of \$100 million and 13% of Total Assets are consistent with Clearwater\'s current standards for this credit profile and reflect the firm\'s assessment of appropriate flexibility. If the issuer draft proposes a general basket in excess of these thresholds, it must be redlined down.
124	
125	**[IV. LIMITATION ON RESTRICTED PAYMENTS]{.underline}**
126	
127	**IV.A --- Builder Basket and Available Amount**
128	
129	**Severity: CRITICAL**
130	
131	**Position.** The builder basket (sometimes referred to as the \"Available Amount\" or the \"cumulative credit\") should start at a base amount of **\$50 million** (the \"Starter Amount\") and grow by **50% of Consolidated Net Income** (if positive; with no reduction for periods of negative Consolidated Net Income unless the Issuer so elects) for each fiscal quarter commencing with the first full fiscal quarter following the Issue Date, plus certain other customary amounts (including, without limitation, the aggregate net cash proceeds received from issuances of Equity Interests of the Issuer to the extent not constituting Excluded Contributions, and returns of capital on or from Restricted Investments previously made using the Available Amount).
132	
133	**Minimum Ratio Requirement.** The Issuer must satisfy a minimum Fixed Charge Coverage Ratio of **2.00 to 1.00** after giving pro forma effect to any restricted payment made pursuant to the builder basket. This ratio test serves as a gating condition --- no restricted payment may be made under the builder basket unless the Issuer can demonstrate, on a pro forma basis, that the Fixed Charge Coverage Ratio would remain at or above 2.00x after giving effect to such payment. The pro forma calculation must include the restricted payment itself (as a reduction to cash or an increase in debt, as applicable) and any related transactions (e.g., the incurrence of Indebtedness to fund the restricted payment).
134	
135	**Excluded Contributions --- Mandatory Exclusion from Available Amount.** The definition of \"Available Amount\" must **NOT** include the aggregate net cash proceeds received from Excluded Contributions. This is a firm and non-negotiable position. Excluded Contributions are equity investments that have been specifically designated by the Issuer as \"Excluded Contributions\" in order to be exempt from the general restricted payments test. They represent a separate capacity to make restricted payments --- the Issuer designates equity proceeds as Excluded Contributions, and those proceeds may then be used to make restricted payments, investments, or other transactions that would otherwise be restricted, without counting against the builder basket, the general RP basket, or any other RP capacity.
136	
137	Allowing Excluded Contributions to also feed the Available Amount would create an impermissible double-counting mechanism. The same dollars would bypass the restricted payments test via the Excluded Contributions carve-out AND simultaneously inflate the Available Amount used to justify additional restricted payments under the builder basket. This is a frequently litigated structural issue in high-yield indentures, and its correction is a firm \"must-have\" for Clearwater Securities. If the issuer draft includes Excluded Contributions as a component of the Available Amount calculation, the relevant clause must be deleted.
138	
139	**Rationale:**
140	
141	> • The Available Amount / builder basket is the primary mechanism by which issuers justify restricted payments over time. Its integrity depends on the accuracy and exclusivity of its inputs.
142	>
143	> • Including Excluded Contributions in the Available Amount permits unlimited leakage by recycling designated equity proceeds through both the Excluded Contributions basket and the builder basket, effectively doubling their utility.
144	>
145	> • This is a frequently litigated issue, and Clearwater has observed multiple instances in recent healthcare transactions where issuer\'s counsel has attempted to include Excluded Contributions in the Available Amount without flagging the structural implication.
146	>
147	> • Any issuer resistance on this point must be escalated to the supervising partner and the Clearwater deal team.
148	
149	**IV.B --- General Restricted Payments Basket**
150	
151	**Severity: SIGNIFICANT**
152	
153	**Position.** The general or catch-all restricted payments basket must not exceed **\$75 million**. This basket functions as a free-and-clear capacity permitting restricted payments without satisfying any ratio test, builder basket availability condition, or other financial prerequisite. Because it operates independently of the financial covenant framework, it must be tightly sized to prevent excessive value leakage to equity holders and affiliates at the expense of noteholders.
154	
155	**Common Issuer Tactic.** Issuers and their counsel frequently propose general restricted payments baskets in the range of \$100 million to \$150 million or higher, often justified by reference to the Issuer\'s dividend policy, management equity program, or anticipated return of capital needs. These justifications do not override the playbook standard. Any amount above \$75 million must be redlined down, and the deviation should be classified as Significant. If the issuer draft proposes a general RP basket in excess of \$125 million, escalate to the partner in addition to redlining, as this suggests an aggressive posture by issuer\'s counsel that may be indicative of broader package concerns.
156	
157	**[V. LIMITATION ON ASSET SALES]{.underline}**
158	
159	**V.A --- Fair Market Value Determination**
160	
161	**Severity: SIGNIFICANT**
162	
163	**Position.** Fair market value for all Asset Sales must be determined by a resolution of the Board of Directors of the Issuer, set forth in an Officer\'s Certificate delivered to the Trustee, stating that such Asset Sale is for fair market value and that the consideration received is at least equal to such fair market value. For any Asset Sale with a fair market value **exceeding \$50 million**, the Issuer must, in addition to delivering the Board resolution and Officer\'s Certificate, obtain an **independent appraisal** from a nationally recognized independent appraisal or valuation firm. The appraisal must be delivered to the Trustee and must confirm that the consideration to be received by the Issuer or the applicable Restricted Subsidiary is at least equal to the fair market value of the assets being disposed of.
164	
165	**Rationale:**
166	
167	> • Board resolutions alone provide insufficient independent verification for large dispositions. Directors may face conflicts of interest, time pressure, or informational asymmetries that impair their ability to accurately assess fair market value in connection with significant asset sales.
168	>
169	> • An independent appraisal requirement protects noteholders against below-market transfers that impair collateral value and enterprise value, particularly in the context of dispositions to affiliates, related parties, or acquirers with pre-existing relationships with the Issuer\'s management or sponsors.
170	>
171	> • The \$50 million threshold balances administrative burden with investor protection. Asset sales below \$50 million do not justify the cost and time associated with a formal independent appraisal; for such transactions, a Board resolution and Officer\'s Certificate provide adequate governance.
172	>
173	> • In healthcare transactions, the valuation of hospital facilities, outpatient centers, and physician practice groups can be complex and fact-specific, making independent verification particularly important.
174	
175	**V.B --- Net Proceeds Application and Reinvestment Period**
176	
177	**Severity: CRITICAL**
178	
179	**Position.** One hundred percent (100%) of Net Proceeds from Asset Sales must be applied to (i) an Offer to Purchase Notes at par (plus accrued and unpaid interest), (ii) the prepayment of Pari Passu Indebtedness (with a corresponding permanent reduction in commitments thereunder, to the extent applicable), or (iii) reinvestment in Replacement Assets (meaning long-term assets of a nature similar to those disposed of and used or useful in the business of the Issuer or its Restricted Subsidiaries), in each case within **365 days** from the date of receipt of such Net Proceeds.
180	
181	**No Extension.** No extension of the reinvestment period shall be permitted, including for \"committed projects,\" \"binding commitments,\" \"signed letters of intent,\" or similar concepts. This is a firm and non-negotiable position. Extensions are one of the most frequently requested issuer modifications to the asset sale covenant, and they are routinely proposed in various forms. The most common form is a 180-day extension for Net Proceeds that are subject to a binding commitment to reinvest at the end of the initial 365-day period --- effectively extending the total reinvestment window to 545 days (approximately 18 months). Such extensions create uncertainty for noteholders, delay the application of proceeds, and effectively undermine the 365-day standard.
182	
183	**Rationale:**
184	
185	> • Extensions (commonly 180 days for \"committed projects\") create uncertainty and effectively extend the reinvestment window to 545 days, well beyond acceptable limits for a secured high-yield notes offering.
186	>
187	> • A clean 365-day window is the firm standard and reflects current market expectations for secured high-yield notes. It provides ample time for the Issuer to identify and execute on reinvestment opportunities without permitting indefinite retention of asset sale proceeds.
188	>
189	> • Extensions are a frequent issuer ask, often packaged with other \"flexibility\" provisions in the asset sale covenant, and must be resisted.
190	
191	**V.C --- Excluded Asset Sale Thresholds**
192	
193	**Severity: MODERATE**
194	
195	**Position.** The indenture should include customary per-transaction and annual aggregate exclusion thresholds below which Asset Sales are not subject to the Net Proceeds application requirements described above. The per-transaction exclusion threshold should be **\$15 million** (i.e., any single Asset Sale with aggregate consideration of \$15 million or less is excluded from the covenant). The annual aggregate exclusion threshold should be **\$40 million** (i.e., the aggregate fair market value of all excluded Asset Sales in any fiscal year may not exceed \$40 million). These thresholds define the scope of Asset Sales to which the Net Proceeds application, reinvestment, and Offer to Purchase mechanics apply.
196	
197	**Note.** These are customary thresholds for issuers of this credit profile and are consistent with recent precedent in the BB/Ba secured healthcare space. If the issuer draft matches these thresholds, no markup is needed. If the draft proposes thresholds that are higher or lower, assess the deviation in context and apply the Moderate severity classification.
198	
199	**[VI. LIMITATION ON TRANSACTIONS WITH AFFILIATES]{.underline}**
200	
201	**Severity: SIGNIFICANT**
202	
203	**Position.** The affiliate transactions covenant must include tiered approval thresholds that provide escalating levels of independent scrutiny for transactions of increasing magnitude:
204	
205	> • **Transactions exceeding \$15 million:** Any transaction or series of related transactions with an Affiliate of the Issuer involving aggregate consideration in excess of \$15 million must be approved by a resolution of a majority of the Board of Directors, including a **majority of the independent (disinterested) directors** then serving on the Board. The Board resolution must be set forth in an Officer\'s Certificate delivered to the Trustee and must certify that the terms of the transaction are no less favorable to the Issuer or the applicable Restricted Subsidiary than those that would be obtained in a comparable arm\'s-length transaction with an unrelated third party.
206	>
207	> • **Transactions exceeding \$40 million:** Any transaction or series of related transactions with an Affiliate of the Issuer involving aggregate consideration in excess of \$40 million must, in addition to Board approval (including independent director approval) as described above, be supported by a **fairness opinion** from an independent financial advisor of nationally recognized standing. The fairness opinion must be delivered to the Trustee and must opine that the transaction is fair, from a financial point of view, to the Issuer or the applicable Restricted Subsidiary.
208	
209	**Rationale:**
210	
211	> • Affiliate transactions present inherent conflicts of interest and are a primary mechanism for value extraction from the issuer credit group to the detriment of noteholders and other creditors.
212	>
213	> • In healthcare transactions, affiliate relationships are particularly common and complex. Hospital operators frequently engage in transactions with affiliated management companies, physician practice groups, ambulatory surgery center joint ventures, shared services organizations, and real estate entities controlled by common sponsors or management. These relationships must be carefully policed to ensure that value is not being transferred out of the restricted group on non-arm\'s-length terms.
214	>
215	> • Lowered thresholds ensure that a broader range of affiliate transactions receive independent scrutiny, reducing the risk that individually small but collectively significant transactions escape the covenant framework.
216	>
217	> • Issuers frequently push for Board approval thresholds of \$25 million or higher and fairness opinion thresholds of \$50 million to \$75 million or higher. These elevated thresholds materially reduce the scope of independent oversight and must be resisted.
218	
219	**Common Issuer Tactics.** Watch for the following:
220	
221	> \(a\) Inflated dollar thresholds for Board approval and fairness opinion requirements, which reduce the number of transactions subject to independent review;
222	>
223	> \(b\) Removal of the independent director majority requirement, leaving affiliate transaction approval to the full Board (which may include directors affiliated with the sponsor or management);
224	>
225	> \(c\) Fairness opinion thresholds set so high as to be practically meaningless --- e.g., \$75 million or higher, which in the context of a mid-cap healthcare issuer would apply to very few transactions;
226	>
227	> \(d\) Overly broad exclusions from the affiliate transaction covenant (e.g., exclusions for \"arm\'s-length\" transactions without any objective verification mechanism, or exclusions for transactions approved by management without Board involvement).
228	
229	**[VII. CHANGE OF CONTROL]{.underline}**
230	
231	**Severity: CRITICAL**
232	
233	**Position.** The Change of Control definition must include all of the following triggers, and the inclusion of each is a non-negotiable requirement:
234	
235	**Continuing Directors Provision.** A Change of Control must be triggered if a majority of the Board of Directors of the Issuer ceases to consist of Continuing Directors. For these purposes, \"Continuing Directors\" means (i) individuals who were members of the Board of Directors on the Issue Date, and (ii) individuals whose nomination for election or appointment to the Board of Directors was approved by a vote of a majority of the then-Continuing Directors at the time of such nomination. This provision protects noteholders against creeping takeovers, hostile proxy contests, and other forms of board reconstitution that occur without a formal acquisition or change-of-control transaction. It ensures that a fundamental shift in governance triggers the repurchase obligation even in the absence of a share acquisition or merger.
236	
237	**Back-End Merger / Asset Sale Trigger.** The Change of Control definition must trigger upon any sale, transfer, conveyance, lease, or other disposition (in one transaction or a series of related transactions) of **\"all or substantially all\"** of the assets of the Issuer and the Restricted Subsidiaries, taken as a whole, to any Person other than a Restricted Subsidiary of the Issuer. The trigger must NOT be defined as a sale of \"more than 50% of consolidated total assets\" or any other percentage-based threshold. The \"all or substantially all\" standard is intentionally imprecise and has been construed broadly by courts, providing noteholders with significantly greater protection than a fixed-percentage test.
238	
239	A 50%-of-assets threshold is materially more permissive than \"all or substantially all.\" Under a percentage-based test, the Issuer could divest up to 49.9% of its consolidated total assets through a merger, reorganization, or series of dispositions without triggering the Change of Control repurchase obligation --- stripping noteholders of a critical protection at the very moment when the most material value is being transferred out of the credit group. The \"substantially all\" standard, by contrast, provides no bright-line safe harbor and requires a facts-and-circumstances analysis that is inherently more protective of noteholders.
240	
241	**Repurchase Offer.** Upon a Change of Control, the Issuer must be required to make an offer to repurchase all outstanding Notes at a purchase price equal to **101% of the aggregate principal amount** thereof, plus accrued and unpaid interest to, but not including, the date of repurchase. The repurchase offer must be commenced within 30 days following the Change of Control and must remain open for at least 20 business days.
242	
243	**Rationale:**
244	
245	> • The Change of Control put is one of the most fundamental protections in a high-yield indenture. It ensures that noteholders have the right to exit the investment at par (plus a 1% premium) in the event of a fundamental change in the ownership or governance of the Issuer.
246	>
247	> • A 50%-of-assets threshold is materially more permissive than the \"substantially all\" standard and must not be accepted. This is a frequent area of issuer negotiation, and issuer\'s counsel may argue that a percentage-based test provides \"certainty\" --- but certainty in this context favors the issuer at the expense of noteholders.
248	>
249	> • The \"continuing directors\" provision protects against scenarios in which control changes without any formal acquisition transaction (e.g., through a proxy contest, consent solicitation, or incremental board appointments over time).
250	>
251	> • Deviations from these positions are unacceptable. Any issuer draft that omits the continuing directors provision or replaces the \"substantially all\" standard with a percentage-based test must be marked up as a Critical item.
252	
253	**[VIII. REPORTING COVENANT]{.underline}**
254	
255	**Severity: CRITICAL**
256	
257	**Position.** The Issuer must covenant to provide the following financial statements and certificates to the Trustee and, upon request, to holders of the Notes:
258	
259	> • **Annual Financial Statements.** Within **90 days** after the end of each fiscal year, audited consolidated financial statements of the Issuer and its Restricted Subsidiaries, including a consolidated balance sheet, consolidated statement of income, consolidated statement of cash flows, and consolidated statement of stockholders\' equity, together with the related notes thereto, all prepared in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles (\"GAAP\") consistently applied, and audited by an independent registered public accounting firm of nationally recognized standing. The auditor\'s report must contain an unqualified opinion (or, in the case of a \"going concern\" qualification only, an opinion so qualified).
260	>
261	> • **Quarterly Financial Statements.** Within **45 days** after the end of each of the first three fiscal quarters of each fiscal year, unaudited consolidated financial statements of the Issuer and its Restricted Subsidiaries, including a consolidated balance sheet, consolidated statement of income, and consolidated statement of cash flows, together with the related notes thereto (which may be condensed or summary notes), all prepared in accordance with GAAP consistently applied, subject to normal year-end audit adjustments and the absence of footnotes. Quarterly financial statements must be reviewed (but need not be audited) by the Issuer\'s independent registered public accounting firm in accordance with Statement on Auditing Standards No. 100 (or any successor standard).
262	>
263	> • **Compliance Certificate.** Accompanying each set of annual and quarterly financial statements, a certificate (the \"Compliance Certificate\") signed by the Chief Financial Officer or the Chief Executive Officer of the Issuer, certifying (a) that the Issuer is in compliance with all covenants contained in the Indenture (or, if not, specifying the nature of the non-compliance and the steps being taken to cure it), (b) a detailed computation of the Fixed Charge Coverage Ratio and the Consolidated Total Leverage Ratio as of the end of the relevant period, and (c) whether any Default or Event of Default has occurred during the period covered by such financial statements and, if so, the nature thereof and the actions taken or proposed to be taken by the Issuer with respect thereto.
264	
265	**Blackout / Suspension Rights: NONE.** The indenture must **not** contain any provision permitting the Issuer to suspend, delay, or \"black out\" its reporting obligations for any reason, including but not limited to claims of material disadvantage, competitive harm, pending transactions, material non-public information, securities law considerations, or similar justifications. Any such provision must be deleted in its entirety. This is a firm and non-negotiable position, and it applies regardless of the duration, scope, or conditions attached to the proposed suspension right.
266	
267	**Rationale:**
268	
269	> • Reporting obligations are the foundation of covenant compliance monitoring. Without timely and complete financial information, noteholders and the Trustee cannot determine whether the Issuer is in compliance with the financial tests and covenants contained in the Indenture.
270	>
271	> • Blackout or suspension provisions create information asymmetry between the Issuer and noteholders. During a suspension period, the Issuer\'s management possesses current financial information while noteholders are left to rely on stale data. This asymmetry is particularly dangerous in distressed or deteriorating credit situations --- precisely the circumstances in which timely financial reporting is most needed.
272	>
273	> • Clearwater Securities has a firm \"no exceptions\" policy on reporting suspension rights. This position has been communicated to the institutional investor community and is a baseline expectation of Clearwater-led offerings.
274	>
275	> • Even \"good faith\" qualified blackout provisions --- for example, provisions that permit a suspension only if the Issuer\'s Board of Directors determines in good faith that disclosure would be materially detrimental to the Issuer --- are unacceptable because they vest unfettered discretion in the Issuer\'s management to determine when and whether noteholders receive financial information to which they are contractually entitled.
276	
277	**[IX. EVENTS OF DEFAULT]{.underline}**
278	
279	**IX.A --- Cross-Default (NOT Cross-Acceleration)**
280	
281	**Severity: CRITICAL**
282	
283	**Position.** The Events of Default article must include a **cross-default** provision --- NOT a cross-acceleration provision. The provision must state that an Event of Default occurs under the Indenture if the Issuer or any Restricted Subsidiary defaults in the payment when due of principal of, or fails to observe or perform any other agreement or condition contained in, any Indebtedness of the Issuer or any Restricted Subsidiary having an outstanding principal amount in excess of the threshold amount (as set forth below), and such default or failure continues for a period in excess of any applicable grace period. The threshold amount must be **\$75 million** of Indebtedness.
284	
285	**Distinction Between Cross-Default and Cross-Acceleration.** The distinction between cross-default and cross-acceleration is fundamental, and the use of a cross-acceleration standard rather than a cross-default standard is unacceptable:
286	
287	> • A **cross-default** triggers an Event of Default under the Indenture when the Issuer defaults on other Indebtedness exceeding the threshold amount, regardless of whether the holders or lenders under such other Indebtedness have actually declared it due and payable prior to its stated maturity (i.e., regardless of whether it has been accelerated). The mere occurrence of the default on the other Indebtedness is sufficient.
288	>
289	> • A **cross-acceleration** triggers an Event of Default under the Indenture only when other Indebtedness has been declared due and payable prior to its stated maturity --- i.e., only when it has been actually accelerated. The default alone is not enough; it must ripen into an acceleration.
290	>
291	> • Cross-acceleration gives the Issuer a \"second chance.\" The Issuer can be in default on other Indebtedness --- a credit event that may signal serious financial distress --- without triggering noteholder remedies, so long as the other lenders choose not to accelerate (or are delayed in accelerating due to intercreditor standstill provisions, waiver negotiations, or other factors). During this period, the Issuer\'s credit quality may be deteriorating rapidly while noteholders have no remedies and, potentially, no information about the default.
292	
293	**Threshold.** The cross-default threshold must be **\$75 million**. This threshold is consistent with the credit profile of the Issuer and provides appropriately scaled protection. Any threshold above \$75 million must be marked down. Issuers and their counsel frequently propose thresholds of \$100 million or higher; such proposals must be resisted and redlined.
294	
295	**IX.B --- Judgment Default**
296	
297	**Severity: SIGNIFICANT**
298	
299	**Position.** An Event of Default must occur upon the entry of one or more final, non-appealable judgments or orders for the payment of money against the Issuer or any Restricted Subsidiary in an aggregate amount in excess of **\$75 million** (to the extent not covered by insurance or indemnification from a creditworthy third party). The judgment default threshold is set at \$75 million, consistent with the cross-default threshold, in order to maintain internal consistency among the Events of Default thresholds. Any threshold above \$75 million must be reviewed and, if not justified by specific circumstances, redlined down.
300	
301	**Common Issuer Tactic.** Proposals of \$100 million or higher thresholds for judgment defaults. In healthcare transactions, judgment risk is elevated due to malpractice exposure, government investigations, and whistleblower actions; a lower threshold is therefore appropriate.
302	
303	**IX.C --- Non-Payment Default Cure Period**
304	
305	**Severity: SIGNIFICANT**
306	
307	**Position.** Cure periods for non-payment defaults (i.e., defaults arising from the Issuer\'s failure to comply with any covenant or agreement contained in the Indenture, other than a failure to pay principal, interest, or premium when due) must not exceed **60 days** after notice from the Trustee or holders of at least 25% in aggregate principal amount of outstanding Notes. This cure period applies to covenant defaults, reporting defaults, and any other non-payment Events of Default for which a cure period is specified.
308	
309	**Rationale.** Extended cure periods --- for example, 90 days or longer --- unduly delay the ability of noteholders to exercise remedies for covenant breaches. A 60-day cure period provides ample time for the Issuer to identify the default, determine whether it can be cured, and take corrective action, while maintaining timely accountability to noteholders. In healthcare transactions, where regulatory and operational complexities can complicate covenant compliance, 60 days is a reasonable and adequate cure period. Proposals for cure periods of 90 days or longer must be redlined.
310	
311	**[X. COLLATERAL PROVISIONS]{.underline}**
312	
313	**X.A --- After-Acquired Property**
314	
315	**Severity: CRITICAL**
316	
317	**Position.** The Issuer must covenant to cause the following after-acquired property to be made subject to the lien securing the Notes (and, to the extent required by the Intercreditor Agreement, subject to the lien securing the Credit Facility on a pari passu basis):
318	
319	> • **After-acquired real property** with a fair market value in excess of \$5 million must be made subject to the lien securing the Notes within **60 days** of the date of acquisition. The Issuer must deliver to the Trustee and the Collateral Agent, within such 60-day period, a mortgage or deed of trust encumbering such real property, together with customary title insurance, surveys, environmental assessments, and local counsel opinions, in each case in form and substance reasonably satisfactory to the Collateral Agent.
320	>
321	> • **After-acquired personal property** (including, without limitation, equity interests in newly formed or acquired subsidiaries, equipment, intellectual property, and accounts receivable) must be made subject to the lien securing the Notes within **30 days** of the date of acquisition, by the delivery of appropriate security agreements, pledge agreements, UCC financing statements, and other perfection documentation to the Collateral Agent.
322	
323	**Rationale:**
324	
325	> • Prompt collateral perfection is essential to maintain the integrity and value of the security package over time, particularly for a growing healthcare issuer that regularly acquires hospital facilities, outpatient centers, physician practices, and related assets. Each acquisition that is not promptly subjected to the collateral lien creates a gap in the security package that directly impairs noteholder recovery in a default or bankruptcy scenario.
326	>
327	> • Extended deadlines --- for example, 90 days or longer for personal property, or 120 days or longer for real property --- create unacceptable windows during which after-acquired assets are unencumbered. During these windows, the assets may be subject to competing liens, seizure by other creditors, or disposition by the Issuer without the protections of the collateral release provisions.
328	>
329	> • The 60-day/30-day framework is the firm standard and reflects best-in-class investor protections for secured high-yield notes. It is achievable in practice --- the Issuer\'s counsel and local counsel have ample time within these periods to prepare and deliver the required collateral documentation --- and is consistent with the deadlines typically required by first-lien revolving credit facilities.
330	
331	**X.B --- Collateral Releases**
332	
333	**Severity: CRITICAL**
334	
335	**Position.** Any release of Collateral with a fair market value **exceeding \$25 million** must require the **consent of the Trustee** (acting in its capacity as Trustee under the Indenture and, if applicable, as Collateral Agent under the Security Documents), in addition to any Officer\'s Certificate or other certifications required by the Indenture. The Trustee must be satisfied, based on the Officer\'s Certificate and such other information as it may reasonably request, that the release complies with the terms of the Indenture and the Security Documents, including without limitation that any required Asset Sale procedures have been followed, that any applicable Net Proceeds are being applied in accordance with the Indenture, and that the release does not violate any other provision of the Indenture or the Security Documents.
336	
337	For releases of Collateral with a fair market value of **\$25 million or less**, an Officer\'s Certificate of the Issuer certifying that the release complies with the Indenture and the Security Documents shall be sufficient, and no Trustee consent shall be required. The Officer\'s Certificate must specify the Collateral being released, the estimated fair market value thereof, the basis for the release (e.g., asset sale, permitted disposition, casualty event), and the applicable Indenture provisions under which the release is authorized.
338	
339	**Rationale:**
340	
341	> • Permitting collateral releases solely on the basis of an Officer\'s Certificate, without any independent check or verification, creates a material risk of improper or unauthorized collateral dilution. The Officer\'s Certificate provides only a self-certification by the Issuer\'s management --- the very parties who may have an incentive to release collateral for purposes that do not benefit the noteholders.
342	>
343	> • The \$25 million threshold provides a practical safe harbor for routine collateral releases (e.g., releases in connection with small asset sales, equipment dispositions, or lease terminations) while ensuring Trustee oversight of material collateral dispositions.
344	>
345	> • This is particularly important in healthcare transactions where real property and major equipment assets may be selectively released in connection with facility divestitures, sale-leaseback transactions, or restructurings. Without Trustee oversight, the Issuer could systematically strip the collateral package of its most valuable assets while complying with the letter but not the spirit of the Indenture.
346	
347	**X.C --- General Collateral Principles**
348	
349	**Severity: SIGNIFICANT** (for general collateral review); individual sub-issues may be Critical
350	
351	**Position.** In addition to the specific collateral provisions addressed in Sections X.A and X.B above, all collateral provisions of the Indenture, the Security Documents, and the Intercreditor Agreement must be reviewed for internal consistency and for compliance with the following general principles:
352	
353	> • The Notes must be secured on a **first-priority, pari passu** basis with the Indebtedness under the Credit Facility. The Intercreditor Agreement must clearly establish the pari passu nature of the liens and must not subordinate the Notes\' lien to the Credit Facility lien in any respect (other than customary intercreditor provisions governing the exercise of remedies, application of proceeds, and similar operational matters).
354	>
355	> • **Excluded assets** must be limited to the following categories: (a) real property with a fair market value below \$5 million individually, (b) motor vehicles and other assets subject to certificate-of-title statutes for which perfection by lien notation is impracticable, and (c) certain governmental permits, licenses, and regulatory approvals to the extent that the pledge thereof is prohibited by applicable law or would result in the termination or revocation of such permits, licenses, or approvals. Any additional categories of excluded assets must be reviewed and, if not justified by legal necessity or practical impediment, challenged.
356	>
357	> • Provisions governing the Collateral Agent\'s duties and protections must be appropriate for a secured notes transaction and must not unduly limit the Trustee/Collateral Agent\'s obligations to the noteholders. In particular, provisions that permit the Collateral Agent to rely conclusively on Officer\'s Certificates without any independent verification, or that exculpate the Collateral Agent from liability for failure to maintain or perfect liens, should be reviewed carefully and, if necessary, revised.
358	>
359	> • Anti-marshaling provisions, if present in the Indenture or the Security Documents, should be **removed or limited** in scope. Associates should flag any broad anti-marshaling language for partner review.
360	
361	**[XI. GUARANTOR COVERAGE AND SUBSIDIARY JOINDER]{.underline}**
362	
363	**Severity: CRITICAL**
364	
365	**Position.** The Indenture must require that any Restricted Subsidiary that meets either of the following criteria must unconditionally guarantee the Issuer\'s obligations under the Notes and execute a supplemental indenture effectuating such guarantee within the time periods specified below:
366	
367	> • The Restricted Subsidiary accounts for more than **5% of the consolidated total assets** of the Issuer and its Restricted Subsidiaries; OR
368	>
369	> • The Restricted Subsidiary accounts for more than **5% of the consolidated revenue** of the Issuer and its Restricted Subsidiaries (in each case, measured as of the end of the most recently completed fiscal quarter for which financial statements are available).
370	
371	Any Restricted Subsidiary that meets either threshold must guarantee the Notes and execute a supplemental indenture within **30 days** of the date on which it first meets such threshold (or, in the case of a newly acquired or newly formed Restricted Subsidiary, within 30 days of the date of such acquisition or formation). The guarantee must be a senior secured guarantee, secured by a first-priority lien on all of the assets of such Guarantor (subject to the excluded assets described in Section X.C above), on a pari passu basis with such Guarantor\'s guarantee of the Credit Facility.
372	
373	**Immaterial Subsidiary Exclusion.** The Indenture may contain a customary exclusion for \"immaterial\" or \"dormant\" subsidiaries, but such exclusion must not exceed **\$25 million in the aggregate** for all excluded subsidiaries combined. This is an aggregate cap, not a per-subsidiary cap. Any per-subsidiary threshold (e.g., \"\$50 million per subsidiary\") must be converted to an aggregate cap. The purpose of the aggregate cap is to prevent the cumulative exclusion of subsidiaries whose individual assets or revenues are below any per-subsidiary threshold but whose combined significance to the credit group is material.
374	
375	**Rationale:**
376	
377	> • Guarantor coverage is a primary structural protection for noteholders in leveraged healthcare transactions. Gaps in guarantor coverage allow value to migrate to unguaranteed subsidiaries through intercompany transactions, asset transfers, and new business development. In a bankruptcy or restructuring, assets held by unguaranteed subsidiaries may not be available to satisfy noteholder claims.
378	>
379	> • The 5% / 5% test (assets or revenue) is the firm standard. Any higher threshold --- for example, a 10% / 10% test --- would permit subsidiaries of meaningful size to remain outside the guarantor group, reducing noteholder recovery prospects. A 10% threshold, in the context of an issuer with \$6 billion in consolidated assets, would permit any subsidiary with assets up to \$600 million to avoid providing a guarantee.
380	>
381	> • Per-subsidiary exclusion thresholds (e.g., \"\$50 million per subsidiary\") rather than aggregate caps are a frequent issuer tactic designed to exclude numerous smaller subsidiaries whose combined assets may be material. In healthcare, where operating subsidiaries are often organized on a per-facility or per-market basis, individual subsidiaries may have assets below a per-subsidiary threshold, but the aggregate assets of all excluded subsidiaries could represent a significant portion of the enterprise.
382	>
383	> • In healthcare transactions, physician practice entities, ambulatory surgery center joint ventures, home health subsidiaries, and other operating entities are frequently organized as separate legal entities. Each may individually fall below a per-subsidiary exclusion threshold while collectively representing a substantial portion of the Issuer\'s revenue and assets.
384	
385	**Acquisition-Specific Note.** For the Cumberland Valley Health Partners acquisition (which is expected to close during the second quarter of 2025), the target entities --- including Cumberland Valley Medical Center, LLC; Cumberland Valley Physician Services, P.A.; and Cumberland Valley Senior Living, Inc. --- must become Guarantors within the time frame specified in the transaction documents (currently expected to be 90 days following the closing of the acquisition). The Indenture must not contain any broader exclusion, carve-out, or delayed joinder provision that would delay or prevent the joinder of the Cumberland Valley entities beyond the agreed 90-day post-closing period. Associates should cross-reference the Indenture provisions against the acquisition agreement and the commitment letter to ensure consistency of the joinder timeline.
386	
387	**[APPENDIX A]{.underline}**
388	
389	**[QUICK REFERENCE TABLE OF KEY THRESHOLDS]{.underline}**
390	
391	The following table summarizes every key threshold in this playbook for ease of reference when comparing against issuer drafts. Reviewing associates should use this table as a quick-reference checklist to identify deviations in the issuer draft and should then consult the applicable section of the playbook for the full rationale and instructions.
392	
393	  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
394	  **\#**         **Provision**                                 **Playbook Position**                           **Common Issuer Positions**         **Severity**
395	  -------------- --------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------------------- ----------------------------------- --------------
396	  1              EBITDA Addback Cap                            25% of Consolidated EBITDA; 18-month run-rate   No cap; 24-month run-rate           Critical
397	
398	  2              Credit Facility Basket                        Greater of \$850M and 1.10x LTM EBITDA          Greater of \$1B+ and 1.25x--1.50x   Critical
399	
400	  3              Ratio Debt Pro Forma Test                     Must include debt being incurred                Silent / not pro forma              Critical
401	
402	  4              General RP Basket                             \$75M                                           \$100M--\$150M                      Significant
403	
404	  5              Available Amount --- Excluded Contributions   Must NOT include                                Included                            Critical
405	
406	  6              Asset Sale Reinvestment Period                365 days, no extension                          365 + 180-day extension             Critical
407	
408	  7              Asset Sale FMV --- Independent Appraisal      Required over \$50M                             Board resolution only               Significant
409	
410	  8              Affiliate Transaction --- Board Approval      \>\$15M                                         \>\$25M                             Significant
411	
412	  9              Affiliate Transaction --- Fairness Opinion    \>\$40M                                         \>\$50M--\$75M                      Significant
413	
414	  10             Change of Control --- Back-End Merger         \"Substantially all\" assets                    \"More than 50%\"                   Critical

418	  12             Judgment Default                              \$75M                                           \$100M                              Significant
419	
420	  13             Non-Payment Cure Period                       60 days max                                     90 days                             Significant
421	
422	  14             After-Acquired Property --- Real              60 days                                         90--120 days                        Critical
423	
424	  15             After-Acquired Property --- Personal          30 days                                         60--90 days                         Critical
425	
426	  16             Collateral Release --- Trustee Consent        Required over \$25M                             Officer\'s Certificate only         Critical
427	
428	  17             Immaterial Subsidiary Exclusion               \$25M aggregate                                 \$50M per subsidiary                Critical
429	
430	  18             Reporting --- Blackout / Suspension           Not permitted                                   180-day suspension                  Critical
431	
432	  19             Annual Financials Deadline                    90 days after FYE                               ---                                 ---
433

435	  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
436	
437	**Instructions.** For each row in the table, compare the corresponding provision of the issuer draft against the Playbook Position column. If the issuer draft deviates from the Playbook Position in the direction of the Common Issuer Positions column (or in any other direction that weakens noteholder protections), mark up the issuer draft in accordance with the severity classification and the detailed instructions in the applicable section of this playbook.
438	
439	**[APPENDIX B]{.underline}**
440	
441	**[SEVERITY CLASSIFICATION GUIDE]{.underline}**
442	
443	All issues identified during the indenture review must be classified according to the following three-tier severity system. The severity classification must be included in every margin comment accompanying a redline markup.
444	
445	**Critical.** A provision that, if not corrected, would materially impair noteholder protections or undermine the fundamental covenant architecture of the Indenture. Critical items are must-have positions. If the Issuer or issuer\'s counsel refuses to accept Clearwater\'s position on a Critical item, the reviewing associate must immediately escalate the issue to the supervising partner at Aldgate & Whitmore and to the Clearwater deal team. No Critical item may be conceded, traded, or compromised without the express prior approval of both the Aldgate & Whitmore supervising partner and the senior Clearwater deal team member responsible for the transaction.
446	
447	**Significant.** A provision that is strongly preferred and represents the current Clearwater Securities standard for high-yield secured notes offerings. Significant items reflect best market practice and are expected to be obtained in the ordinary course. If the Issuer resists a Significant item, the reviewing associate must escalate to the supervising partner for discussion and strategic assessment. Significant items may be traded against other Significant items in the context of broader package negotiations, but only with the express approval of the supervising partner. The rationale for any trade must be documented in writing.
448	
449	**Moderate.** A provision that reflects best practice but where deviation may be tolerable in the context of overall deal dynamics, issuer creditworthiness, market conditions, and other concessions obtained. Moderate items are preferred but not required. If a Moderate item is not pursued or is conceded in negotiations, the reviewing associate must document the rationale for the concession and confirm that the decision was made with the supervising partner\'s knowledge.
450	
451	**Default Rule.** Where multiple severity levels could reasonably apply to a given issue, the reviewing associate must default to the higher classification. When in doubt as to the appropriate classification, escalate to the supervising partner for guidance.
452	
453	**DISTRIBUTION NOTICE**
454	
455	Distribution of this document is limited to Aldgate & Whitmore LLP deal team members assigned to Clearwater Securities engagements and members of the Clearwater Securities leveraged finance team, including the Oakvale Capital Markets and Halstead & Co. syndicate desks to the extent participating as co-managers. This document must not be circulated to any issuer, issuer\'s counsel, investor, or other third party under any circumstances. All copies (electronic and hard copy) must be maintained in accordance with Aldgate & Whitmore\'s document retention and confidentiality policies. Contact David K. Morrow (dmorrow@aldgatewhitmore.com) or Catherine Ng (cng@aldgatewhitmore.com) with any questions regarding this playbook or its application to a specific transaction.
